findings.text: The first paragraph tells a newcomer what Athena is, who it is for, and why it matters. Someone who reads only this paragraph can explain the project.
findings.source: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository. ... It solves the problem of AI edits that arrive unreviewed and unaccountable."

findings.text: The next action is linked from the header. The Next steps section lists prerequisites, the clone command, ./setup.sh and a first command (athena ask "add a changelog"), so the newcomer has a clear path to try Athena.
findings.source: "Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself." and the Next steps section

findings.text: The page lives at Athena's root URL, but almost all of it is a detailed study of a different tool, firstmate. The lede says Athena's job is turning requests into commits, yet the page demonstrates a different ability: reading and explaining a project. It never says how the two connect, so a newcomer may not see why this page is Athena's front door.
findings.source: <title>Athena explains how firstmate handles work</title>; "A study is Athena's written reading of another software project"

findings.text: This header link speaks to the project owner, not a visitor. A newcomer has no proposals and no context for what deciding means here.
findings.source: "Owner view: proposals waiting for your decision."

findings.text: Cost tracing and the model-checks-model review are the stated selling points, but the page shows no example of either: no sample commit, verdict or cost record. The newcomer has to take them on trust until they install.

The walkthrough uses terms like exit 75 and captain call before explaining them, and the Glossary admits "The firstmate source does not define a captain call." A newcomer to firstmate will find this section hard going.
findings.source: Heading "One piece of work, start to finish": "the spawn exits 75"; "If the backlog item is still an open captain call"

findings.text: The card title says there is no concurrency cap, while the transitions describe deferring at capacity. Claim c5 explains that only a declared project capacity limits dispatch, but the card itself reads as a contradiction.
findings.source: ra3 "Dispatch isolated work with no concurrency cap" vs t2 "Every worker place is held, so the spawn is deferred with exit 75"

findings.text: The page says plainly that nothing was executed and that a first reading missed some paths. This honesty about limits helps a careful reader trust the rest.
findings.source: Heading "Limits of this study": "every claim is marked read"; "none was run"

findings.text: This points to a folder without a link or the name of its repository, so a newcomer cannot follow it.
findings.source: Heading "About this page": "the name of the folder under studies/ that holds the data"
